items.title: Avoiding Informal Conversations
items.quote: 1. Avoiding Informal Conversations: 👉 Those casual conversation at work are gold. They help you with exposure to everyday English usage, support the development of natural conversational skills and help you get noticed at work. ✅ So, instead of waiting for others to ask you questions, take the lead., Introduce yourself, open up and try to make “small talk”.

items.title: Overemphasis on Technical Jargon
items.quote: 2. Overemphasis on Technical Jargon: 👉I get it, technical words feel comfortable. You know them and you use them every day. But if you get a blank face or an embarrassed silence? In multicultural settings not everyone may be familiar with complex technical terms. ✅Find the right balance between technical jargon and plain language, and make sure your communication is clear.

items.title: Not Participating in Meetings
items.quote: 3. Not Participating in Meetings: 👉Instead of dreading the next team meeting, take control. Prepare some questions, reflect on your contribution and talk about what you do. ✅This is the best way to build confidence and overcome that fear of making mistakes.

items.title: Lack of Proactive Learning
items.quote: 4. Lack of Proactive Learning: 👉Company courses are good, and they are usually free. But what if they never come? Or if they are too late? Waiting for formal language training can actually slow you down. ✅Take ownership of your language skills and start improving them independently. Be proactive.

items.title: Fear of Feedback
items.quote: 5. Fear of Feedback: 👉Feedback is a powerful tool for growth. Let’s use it effectively to boost our confidence. How? ↳ Be specific. ↳ Choose the right person. ↳ Set a positive tone. ✅Once you get some feedback, create a practical action plan. For instance, if pronunciation is highlighted, practice those specific sounds regularly. Remember, confidence is a skill, and it can be developed and improved. You have more control over it than you think. Am I missing anything? Let me know in the comments.

items.title: Focus on your strengths
items.quote: 1. Focus on your strengths. ➜ Reflect on what makes you unique (not what the others expect of you). Use your style. Do not rush to meet deadlines, demonstrate your skills. 👉 "I believe in taking the time to ensure accuracy and precision in our work, which ultimately leads to better outcomes."

items.title: Refine your language
items.quote: 2. Refine your language. ➜ Learn how to be effective but professional at the same time. Be patient. 👉 “FIRST we’ll discuss the upgrade, THEN we’ll submit it for approval, FINALLY, we’ll implement it” “could you please help me with my report?”

items.title: Find a mentor
items.quote: 3. Find a mentor. ➜ Seek guidance and support as well as valuable feedback. Learn from the best. 👉 “I've been really impressed by your expertise. Would you be open to sharing your insights and guidance with me as I navigate my career path in IT?”

items.title: Build a network
items.quote: 4. Build a network. ➜ Be open with your peers, colleagues and management. Join virtual (social network) and real networks. Make the most of company events and use “small talk”. 👉 "Hi there! How are you finding the event so far? I noticed your name badge - are you part of the Finance department? Have you been to similar events before?"

items.title: Be active in team meetings
items.quote: 5. Be active in team meetings. ➜ Ask questions, volunteer to present part of the agenda, offer to take notes, contribute with well-thought questions. 👉 “I've been thinking about our current project, and I believe we could improve the UX integrating the new layout. What are your thoughts on this?"

items.title: Make the most of your 1 to 1’s
items.quote: 6. Make the most of your 1 to 1’s ➜ Listen to and use the feedback you receive. Make sure you share your expectations and growth plan with your leader. If you keep silent, they won’t know. 👉 “Could we schedule some time to discuss potential opportunities for development and how I can best align my goals with the team's objectives?"

items.title: Make your work visible
items.quote: 7. Make your work visible. ➜ It’s not only about doing the work. But also making sure people know. Talk & write about it. Ask for 5 minutes in your next team meeting, write a newsletter, email your leader asking for advice. 👉 "I wanted to share an update on the project that I've been working on. The first test was successful, and I believe we’re on the right track."

items.title: Take care of yourself
items.quote: 8. Take care of yourself. ➜ Stay active both mentally and physically. Mind your own wellbeing so it reflects at work. 👉 “I've been implementing deep breathing and short breaks to help manage stress levels during busy periods, and I've found it really beneficial." items.title: Unemployed
items.quote: 1. Unemployed Definition: Not having a job. Example: "After the company downsized, several IT professionals found themselves unemployed and started looking for new opportunities."

items.title: Self-Employed
items.quote: 2. Self-Employed Definition: Working for oneself as a freelancer or the owner of a business rather than for an employer. Example: "After years in corporate IT, Sarah decided to become self-employed and started her own cybersecurity consulting firm."

items.title: Part-Time
items.quote: 3. Part-Time Definition: Working fewer hours than a full-time job, often less than 35 hours a week. Example: "To balance his studies and work, John took a part-time position as a junior developer at a tech startup."

items.title: Temporary
items.quote: 4. Temporary Definition: Working for a limited period. Example: "During the project implementation phase, we hired a temporary IT specialist to help manage the increased workload."

items.title: Work For
items.quote: 5. Work For Definition: To be employed by someone or an organization. Example: "I work for a leading software development company, focusing on project management and team coordination."

items.title: To Be in Charge of
items.quote: 6. To Be in Charge of Definition: To have control or responsibility for something. Example: "As the IT manager, I am in charge of overseeing the network infrastructure and ensuring system security."

items.title: To Be Responsible For
items.quote: 7. To Be Responsible For Definition: To have a duty to take care of something or someone. Example: "I am responsible for the performance and development of my team, making sure they meet our project deadlines."

items.title: To Be Sacked (or Fired)
items.quote: 8. To Be Sacked (or Fired) Definition: To be dismissed from a job. Example: "Unfortunately, due to repeated security breaches, the IT director was sacked for failing to protect company data."

items.title: Set Up a Company
items.quote: 9. Set Up a Company Definition: To start a new business. From hospitality to real estate to Finance in large corporations. items.title: Focus on your strengths
items.quote: 1. Focus on your strengths. ➜ Reflect on what makes you unique (not what the others expect of you). Use your style. At the beginning, prioritize quality over quantity (and speed). 👉 "I believe in taking the time to ensure accuracy and precision in my work, which ultimately leads to better outcomes."

items.title: Refine your language
items.quote: 2. Refine your language. ➜ Learn how to be effective but professional at the same time. Be patient. 👉 “FIRST we’ll discuss the upgrade, THEN we’ll submit it for approval, FINALLY, we’ll implement it” “Could you 𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 help me with my report?”

items.title: Find a mentor
items.quote: 3. Find a mentor. ➜ Seek guidance, support and valuable feedback. Learn from the best. 👉 “I'm really impressed by your expertise. Could I ask you a few questions to clarify this process ands maybe get a few extra ideas on my personal development?”

items.title: Build a network
items.quote: 4. Build a network. ➜ Be open with your peers, colleagues and management. Join virtual (social network) and real networks. Make the most of company events and use “small talk”. 👉 "Hi there! How are you finding the event so far? I noticed your name badge - are you part of the Finance department? Have you been to similar events before?"

items.title: Be active in team meetings
items.quote: 5. Be active in team meetings. ➜ Ask questions, volunteer to present part of the agenda, offer to take notes, contribute with well-thought questions. 👉 “I've been thinking about our current project, and I believe we could improve the UX integrating the new layout. What are your thoughts on this?"

items.title: Make the most of your 1 to 1’s
items.quote: 6. Make the most of your 1 to 1’s ➜ Listen to and use the feedback you receive. Make sure you share your expectations and growth plan with your leader. If you keep silent, they won’t know. 👉 “Could we schedule some time to discuss potential opportunities for development and how I can best align my goals with the team's objectives?"

items.title: Make your work visible
items.quote: 7. Make your work visible. ➜ It’s not only about doing the work. But also making sure people know. Talk & write about it. Ask for 5 minutes in your next team meeting, write a newsletter, email your leader asking for advice. 👉 "I wanted to share an update on the project that I've been working on. The first test was successful, and I believe we’re on the right track."

items.title: Take care of yourself
items.quote: 8. Take care of yourself. ➜ Stay active both mentally and physically. Mind your own wellbeing so it reflects at work. 👉 “I've been implementing deep breathing and short breaks to help manage stress levels during busy periods, and I've found it really beneficial." items.title: Reverse the perfectionism cycle by speaking first

tags.label: fear of speaking or sounding silly

items.quote: 👀 “Am I a stalker?” Not exactly 😅 But I do observe a lot. That’s where it all starts: 🟡 Observation. When I talk to professionals, I listen carefully. Not just to their words, but to what’s behind the words. I hear things like: 💬 “My mind goes blank when I speak.” 💬 “I try to say things the right way, but I just feel unsure.” 💬 “I’m scared of sounding silly, so I stay quiet.” And when I observe them at work, I recognize something familiar A cycle I had to break myself when my career hit a wall.

items.title: Apply
items.quote: 🔘 Apply: to request something officially. Example: "John decided to apply for the position of IT project manager at the multinational tech company."

items.title: Do overtime
items.quote: 🔘 Do overtime: working extra hours beyond your normal schedule Example: "Due to the upcoming deadline, the IT team had to do overtime to ensure the successful implementation of the software update."

items.title: Get promoted
items.quote: 🔘 Get promoted: to obtain a higher rank in your job Example: "After years of dedication and hard work, Sarah was finally promoted to the position of IT director."

items.title: Resign
items.quote: 🔘 Resign: voluntarily leave a job Example: "James made the difficult decision to resign from his role as senior software engineer to pursue a new opportunity."

items.title: Retire
items.quote: 🔘 Retire: stop working because you reached a particular age Example: "After a long and successful career in IT, David decided it was time to retire and enjoy his well-deserved rest."

items.title: Run a company
items.quote: 🔘 Run a company: manage a company Example: "As the CEO of the IT consulting firm, Mark was responsible for running the company and overseeing its operations."

items.title: To Be in Charge of
items.quote: 🔘 To Be in Charge of: to have responsibility Example: "As the IT manager, I am in charge of overseeing the network infrastructure and ensuring system security."

items.title: Set up (start)
items.quote: 🔘 Set up (start): establish Example: "The IT team worked tirelessly to set up the new server infrastructure to support the company's growing data needs."

items.title: To be made redundant
items.quote: 🔘 To be made redundant: the company doesn't need you Example: "Unfortunately, due to budget cuts, several employees in the IT department were made redundant."

items.title: To be sacked (also: to be fired)

tags.label: To be sacked (also: to be fired)

items.quote: 🔘 To be sacked (also: to be fired): you've done something wrong Example: "After repeated warnings for poor performance, Alex was eventually sacked from his position as IT support specialist."

items.title: Work shifts
items.quote: 🔘 Work shifts: flexible work schedule Example: "As part of the IT operations team, Sarah had to work shifts to ensure round-the-clock monitoring of the company's network infrastructure."

items.title: Remote Working
items.quote: 🔘Remote Working: Example: "In remote working, employees are located away from the traditional office setting, working from home or other remote locations. They rely on digital communication tools to stay connected with their team".

items.quote: Tech was a lot about information, but not so much about communication. Throughout my years as a CTO, developer, and founder, I encountered this problem frequently. It wasn't the actual technical issues that were holding us back; it was the things in between the people that created Resistance. And communication is the alpha & omega of the process to fix it and, of course, turn it into a stable environment worth being a part of. For this episode, I invited a person worth following: Daniele Ponzo.

items.title: Real English confidence comes from connection, not perfection
items.quote: What’s The Psychology Behind Real English Confidence? A million dollar question. One that’s not easy to answer. I was lucky enough to be invited by Richard Marshall on his podcast “𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗟𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿” to try and answer the question. And I’m truly grateful, because he allowed me to look back into my own experience. It took me right back to when I first landed in Ireland - new country, new culture, new job… and a new language to work in. At the time, I thought confidence came from perfection.

items.title: Small daily practice builds speaking confidence under pressure
items.quote: What happens when we can’t speak? Ok, I don’t mean like Neo in Matrix (the interrogation scene!) 😶 I mean English You’ve studied for years. You can read, you can listen, you can write emails just fine. But the moment you have to speak especially in a meeting, a presentation, or a job interview something happens: 🔴 Your mind goes blank. 🔴 You overthink every word. 🔴 You feel like your voice disappears. Sound familiar? Well, it is. Many professionals feel exactly the same. But it doesn’t mean you’

items.title: Overthinking every word
items.quote: ❌ 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 You start speaking… and suddenly your brain becomes a live coding debugger. “Wait, is that the correct tense? Should I use 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯 or 𝘩𝘢𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘦𝘯?” By the time you decide, the conversation has moved on… twice. ▶️ Tip: Focus on clarity, not grammar perfection. Say it simply and keep the flow.

items.title: Translating word by word
items.quote: ❌ 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱 Ever tried to speak English while mentally translating from your native language? It’s like running Windows inside a Mac. Everything slows down. ▶️ Tip: Train your brain to think in English. Start small. Describe your morning or your lunch without translating first.

items.title: Using “fancy” words to sound smart
items.quote: ❌ 𝗨𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 “𝗳𝗮𝗻𝗰𝘆” 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁 “I am extremely delighted to be in the possession of this magnificent opportunity to address you…” Meanwhile, your audience is thinking: “Wait, what?” ▶️ Tip: Simple language is powerful language. You don’t need fireworks. Just clarity.

items.title: Copying your native language grammar
items.quote: ❌ 𝗖𝗼𝗽𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿 In Italian, Spanish, or French, long sentences full of connectors sound elegant. In English? It can sound like a never-ending maze. By the time you reach the verb, your listener has already gone for coffee. ☕ ▶️ Tip: Keep sentences short. One idea per sentence. Your message will land stronger.

The first test was successful, and I believe we’re on the right track."

items.title: 5 communication breakdown moments for developers
items.quote: title: 5 communication breakdown moments for developers --- You understand everything. Until it’s your turn to speak. items.title: 𝟮. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴

items.title: 𝟯. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴

items.title: 𝟰. 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗿𝘂𝘀𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗱

items.title: Clear Endpoints → Clear Openings
items.quote: 1️⃣ 𝗖𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗘𝗻𝗱𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘀 → 𝗖𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 A good API makes it obvious where to start. Your communication should do the same. Instead of: "Umm... I was thinking that maybe..." Start with: "My recommendation is..." or "The issue is..." People shouldn't have to guess where you're going.

items.title: Predictable Payloads → Predictable Structure
items.quote: 2️⃣ 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱𝘀 → 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 Developers love predictable JSON. Listeners do too. When your message follows a familiar structure, people stop working to understand you and start listening to your ideas. One of my favourites: Issue → Impact → Recommendation Simple. Repeatable. Easy to follow.

items.title: Pagination → Don't Panic Explain
items.quote: 3️⃣ 𝗣𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗗𝗼𝗻'𝘁 𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗰 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗻 No API sends an entire database in one response. Yet that's exactly what many engineers do when they're under pressure. Every edge case. Every dependency. Every technical detail. Instead: Prepare one idea. Deliver it in 1 sentence Pause. Then build from there. Don't overload your audience's processing capacity.

items.title: Graceful Error Handling → Recover Without Panic
items.quote: 4️⃣ 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 → 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗰 Good APIs don't crash because of one exception. Neither should you. If you lose your train of thought, don't apologise. Recover. A simple: "Let me rephrase that." is often all you need. People remember how confidently you recover, not whether you made a small mistake.

items.title: Low Latency → Lower Cognitive Load
items.quote: 5️⃣ 𝗟𝗼𝘄 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 → 𝗟𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗴𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗱 This is the one that matters most. When your brain is translating, checking grammar, searching for vocabulary, and reading the room at the same time... communication latency increases. hesitation appears. you start running around in circles panic explaining starts. expertise becomes harder to hear. The goal isn't perfect English. It's reducing cognitive load. Because when your brain has fewer processes running... your communication becomes faster, clearer,

items.title: Start with direction
items.quote: 1️⃣ 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗱𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Don't make people guess where you're going. ❌ Instead of: "I was just thinking that maybe we could..." ✅ Try: "My recommendation is..." or "The point I'd like to raise is..." The first sentence should reduce uncertainty, not create it.

items.title: Lead with the point
items.quote: 2️⃣ 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 Many professionals explain everything... before saying what they actually mean. History. Background. Exceptions. Technical details. By the time they reach the point... the room has already moved on. A much better structure is: Point → Reason → Detail For example: "I recommend delaying the release by one week. The main reason is quality risk. We still have two unresolved issues in the payment flow." Simple. Logical. Easy to follow.

items.title: Structure beats certainty
items.quote: 3️⃣ 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘁𝘆 You don't need to sound 100% certain. You do need to sound organised. ❌ "Maybe... I'm not sure... perhaps..." ✅ "I see two possible options." or "My initial view is..." People don't expect you to know everything. They do expect you to think clearly.

items.title: Finish with a recommendation
items.quote: 4️⃣ 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 Senior communication doesn't stop at information. It ends with direction. Instead of finishing with: "So... that's the situation." Finish with: ✅ "My recommendation is..." ✅ "The next step is..." ✅ "What I'd suggest is..." Never leave people wondering: "So... what do we do now?"

items.title: Replace filler words with pauses
items.quote: 5️⃣ 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗽𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲𝘀 When your brain needs a second... don't fill the silence. ❌ "Uhm..." "Basically..." "You know..." "How can I say..." Pause. Think. Continue. A short pause sounds far more confident than a sentence full of filler words.

items.quote: 3️⃣ Set micro targets.
